title: Private egress SNI timing + replay experiments
content:
Purpose:
Quick personal lab notes for reproducing and probing an intermittent TLS handshake failure seen from private deployments when traffic exits via a peered VPC path. This is an exploratory scratchpad — command outputs, small traces, failed/success scenarios, and hypotheses for next steps.

Summary of the symptom:
- Customer private deployment (VPC A) -> Peered VPC B (egress NAT/egress cluster) -> external target (api.example.com).
- ~1-3% of requests observe TLS handshake stall / client timeout around ClientHello->ServerHello (client times out at ~4s). Subsequent immediate retry succeeds. Not correlated with token size.
- Observable in app logs as: "tls: handshake did not complete: deadline exceeded" and in reverse-proxy as "upstream read timeout".

What I attempted (timestamped experiments):
- 2025-02-14 09:10 - baseline DNS and reachability
  dig +short api.example.com @10.0.0.2 -> 172.31.200.45
  curl -v --connect-timeout 5 --max-time 10 https://api.example.com/health --resolve api.example.com:443:172.31.200.45
  -> 95% success, occasional curl: (35) SSL connect error: Resource temporarily unavailable

- 2025-02-14 09:35 - low-level TCP/TLS repro
  # open raw TCP to observe timing
  time (echo -n | openssl s_client -connect 172.31.200.45:443 -servername api.example.com -alpn h2) 2>&1 | tee sni_repro.log
  s_client sometimes prints nothing for 4s then aborts with 'connect: Resource temporarily unavailable' or a partial handshake with no ServerHello.

- 2025-02-14 10:20 - try forcing different SNI values to see server behavior
  openssl s_client -connect 172.31.200.45:443 -servername api.example.com 
  openssl s_client -connect 172.31.200.45:443 -servername other.example.com
  Observed: api.example.com sometimes succeeds, other.example.com returns TLS alert (unrelated). Not deterministic.

- 2025-02-14 11:00 - packet capture on node inside VPC A (client side) and in peered VPC B (egress node).
  tcpdump -i eth0 host 172.31.200.45 and port 443 -w client-side.pcap
  tcpdump -i eth1 host 172.31.200.45 and port 443 -w egress-side.pcap
  Observations: when handshakes fail, we still see the TCP 3-way handshake and a ClientHello on the wire from the client. ServerHello rarely visible from egress-side capture in failing cases. No obvious RSTs.

- 2025-02-14 12:10 - asymmetric path / ECMP hypothesis test
  traceroute -T -p 443 172.31.200.45
  -> path A -> path B occasional alternation when repeated quickly. ECMP hash seems to split packets at client-source-port variation.
  ip route get 172.31.200.45
  -> via 10.0.2.1 dev eth0 src 10.0.1.10

- 2025-02-14 13:00 - TLS record size / PMTU angle
  curl --http2 --max-time 10 -v https://api.example.com --header "X-Debug: pmtu-test" --tcp-nodelay
  -> Failures still occur. MTU on tunnel: 9001, but peering link MTU 1500. Fragmentation doesn't look evident in pcap samples.

- 2025-02-14 14:00 - NAT/connection reuse probe
  # Make many parallel connections with same source IP/port pattern
  for i in {1..200}; do curl -sS -k https://api.example.com/health & done; wait
  -> Failure rate increases to ~4% during burst. Suggests connection tracking or port exhaustion effect.

Notes from captures (select snippets):
- Client-side (failing case):
  10:12:03.123456 IP 10.0.1.10.53912 > 172.31.200.45.443: Flags [S], seq 0
  10:12:03.123506 IP 172.31.200.45.443 > 10.0.1.10.53912: Flags [S.], ack 1
  10:12:03.123530 IP 10.0.1.10.53912 > 172.31.200.45.443: Flags [.], ack 1
  10:12:03.124000 IP 10.0.1.10.53912 > 172.31.200.45.443: Flags [P.], seq 1:534, ack 1
  (ClientHello payload present)

- Egress-side (same time, failing case):
  10:12:03.123800 IP 10.0.1.10.53912 > 172.31.200.45.443: Flags [P.], seq 1:534, ack 1
  (No ServerHello observed in the next 5s capture window)

- Successful case capture: we see ServerHello at 10:12:03.124120.

Interpreting the timing:
- The client sends ClientHello immediately after handshake establishment. In failing traces, server does not reply (or reply does not arrive on egress tap). This implies either server never receives ClientHello (dropped in transit inside peered path) OR server replies but reply takes different path and is lost to our egress tap (asymmetric return path).

Hypotheses (ranked):
1) ECMP/asymmetric routing causing ClientHello to hit a node that forwards towards the server while response is routed back to a different egress NAT (no state) -> server's ServerHello lost. Evidence: traceroute alternation; burst increases failure rate.
2) Connection tracking / NAT hairpinning problem on the peered egress cluster: some NAT instances are not replicating conntrack state for forwarded TCP 1st packet so server's reply goes to instance without state -> dropped. Evidence: failure increases under parallel connections; no RSTs but no ServerHello.
3) SNI rewrite / proxy alive-check interference: some layer 7 proxies in peered VPC inject or inspect TLS, and under load their TLS handoff times out. Less likely because we see ClientHello at egress and server not replying.
4) MTU/fragmentation causing TLS handshake (large ClientHello with many ALPN/extension) to be fragmented and dropped by intermediate firewall/NAT that does not reassemble correctly. Evidence weak: packet captures show single TCP segment usually < MSS.

Repro plan (next steps):
- Controlled ECMP isolation: force single path by setting source port and pinning flow so ECMP doesn't split. Use h1 flow label (if available) or temporarily adjust route to point to single nexthop. See whether failure disappears.
- Conntrack logging on each egress NAT node: enable nf_conntrack logging for tcp syns and syn-acks; correlate with the times of failing ClientHellos.
- Run PCAP on the actual server-side NIC (if permitted) to confirm whether ClientHello arrived at server. If it did, problem likely on server/app side. If it didn't, issue is in the peered network.
- Increase sampling of small intervals during bursts to see pattern vs source port reuse.

Quick experiments to run tomorrow: one-liners to reproduce quickly
- Reproduce with fixed 1s spacing for connection attempts:
  for i in {1..200}; do sleep 0.01; curl -sS --http2 --resolve api.example.com:443:172.31.200.45 https://api.example.com/health & done; wait

- Pin source port to simulate client reuse (requires raw sockets or socat):
  socat - TCP:172.31.200.45:443,sourceport=53912,servername=api.example.com

- SNI replay with payload variations (test extension bloat):
  openssl s_client -connect 172.31.200.45:443 -servername api.example.com -tlsextdebug -nbio_test

Potential mitigations if hypothesis 1/2 confirmed:
- Ensure conntrack/forwarding state is synchronized or sticky routing for flows (hashing by 5-tuple) so reply goes back through the same NAT instance.
- Add short client-side retry with jitter for private deployments as a pragmatic mitigation while infra fix rolls out (already partially implemented).

Notes & oddities:
- Some failing traces show server eventually sending ServerHello after ~6s (client already timed out). Suggests server-side slowness under certain egress path conditions — need server-side metrics.
- Failure not correlated with specific client instance — appears across many private nodes.
- AWS VPC peering has no native NAT — peered route to a dedicated egress cluster implies we run our own NAT/egress proxies in the peered VPC. Those proxies are where I suspect state divergence.

Known tickets / context:
- JIRA-PI-2142: "Intermittent TLS handshake timeouts from private deployments" (linked).
- Recent change: egress cluster autoscale introduced a stateless proxy/edge to improve scale (mid-Jan 2025). Hypothesis: autoscaler introduced multi-instance forwarding without state sync.

Action items (me):
- [ ] Add conntrack logging and rotate to short retention for a 2-hour window during reproduced test.
- [ ] Coordinate with infra to capture server NIC pcap during controlled repro window.
- [ ] Run ECMP pinning test to confirm asymmetric path hypothesis.
- [ ] If confirmed, propose sticky-hash for peered egress traffic and/or ensure stateful proxy placement.

If you pick this up: look for correlation between source-port reuse pattern and the failing ClientHello times. Also check if any WAF/inspection box in peered path has been updated mid-Jan.

Random aside: I noticed some of the failing ClientHello packets include many ALPN values (h2,http/1.1,acme-tls/1). Try pruning ALPN in repro client to see if it reduces size and failure rate.

End of scratchpad.
